I am 71 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou for half a century. My bones ache in the morning, and with only the two of us at home, I cannot afford to gamble on fancy new methods or crops that demand too much bending and spraying. I know my 12 mu like the back of my hand. The wheat-maize rotation on 10 mu is our foundation—it puts food on the table and leaves us with grain to sell. I will rotary till before sowing winter wheat, using improved seed such as Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22, because these varieties have proven themselves here year after year. I apply compound fertilizer as a base and topdress with urea at green-up and jointing; our well gives us water for three irrigations, which is enough if we time them right. When the wheat comes off in early June, I plant hybrid maize—Denghai 605, same as my neighbors—directly into the stubble without tilling. Maize is forgiving, but it needs two good irrigations and careful weeding. The remaining 2 mu I keep in cotton. Cotton means more labor, especially all those insecticide sprays for bollworm, but the income helps with our medicine and daily costs. I rotary till the cotton plot in spring, plant an improved variety like Guoxinmian, irrigate twice, and stay on top of the pests. At my age, I do not chase record yields; I chase harvests that do not break my back or my wallet.
